metadata.title: Texas Is Holding $9 Billion+ in Unclaimed Money. Some Is Oil Royalties
metadata.author: Royalty Clerk
metadata.shortDescription:
The Texas Comptroller holds more than $9 billion in unclaimed property, and part of it is oil and gas royalty money that never reached the owner. Here's how royalties go missing, who it happens to, how to search ClaimItTexas.gov like a detective, how to claim, the 10% finder-fee cap in Texas law, and how to keep it from happening again.

Free tools from Royalty Clerk:
- Unclaimed royalties search: https://royaltyclerk.com/tools/unclaimed-royalties-search?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=v2
- Texas unclaimed royalties guide: https://royaltyclerk.com/texas-unclaimed-royalties?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=v2
- Mineral interest finder: https://royaltyclerk.com/tools/mineral-interest-finder?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=v2

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:32 How royalties go missing
1:17 Who this happens to
1:53 How to search
2:30 Search like a detective
3:48 How to claim
4:29 The finder trap
5:10 Make it stop
5:40 Free tools

General information, not legal, tax or investment advice. Sample numbers, families and documents are illustrations, not real owners. For your own situation, talk to a Texas oil and gas or probate attorney.

Royalty Clerk: public records for Texas mineral and royalty owners. https://royaltyclerk.com?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=v2

metadata.title: Unclaimed Property Explained: How To Check and Claim It
metadata.author: Hoang Le CFP, EA, Real Estate Agent
metadata.shortDescription:
Unclaimed property is money and assets — old bank accounts, uncashed checks, insurance payouts, stock dividends, and more — that a company or agency couldn't deliver to you and was legally required to hand over to the state. It never expires, but finding and claiming it takes a few deliberate steps. 

- What counts: dormant bank accounts, uncashed paychecks, matured life insurance, stock dividends, utility deposits, and abandoned safe deposit box contents 
- Dormancy periods vary by asset type: wages and utility deposits typically go unclaimed after 1 year; most accounts and life insurance after 3–5 years; some categories up to 15 years 
- Search every state you've ever lived or worked in, plus the free national database MissingMoney.com 
- Don't skip federal sources: IRS Where's My Refund, the PBGC pension database, FDIC failed-bank funds, and TreasuryDirect's Treasury Hunt for savings bonds 
- Filing a legitimate claim is always free and typically requires your Social Security number, ID, and for larger or inherited claims, notarized documentation 
- Watch for scams: legitimate searches never charge upfront fees, and licensed 'heir finders' are capped around 10% of the property's value 

Disclaimer 
This video is for general informational and educational purposes only and is not legal, tax, or financial advice. Unclaimed property rules, dormancy periods, and documentation requirements vary significantly by state and change over time, so verify current requirements directly on your state's official website, and consult a qualified professional for complex claims involving estates or business compliance.

If this helped you, hit like, subscribe for more practical financial and tax education, and share this with a family member who's moved a few times over the years — they're the most likely to have something waiting for them.

Unclaimed Property Business: Top 8 Key Terms To Understand.

1.) Unclaimed Funds: refer to money or other financial assets that have been abandoned or forgotten by their rightful owners for an extended period. These funds can originate from various sources, such as: Unclaimed Bank Accounts, Insurance Policies & Securities. 

2.) Recovery Agent: An individual or business that assists owners in reclaiming their unclaimed property, often for a fee or percentage of the recovered funds. Also might be know as a Heir Finder or Locator depending on what State they are working in.

3.) Claimant: A person or entity filing that owns the Unclaimed Funds account that's hired you on their behalf to recover it for them.

4.) Holder: The entity (such as a bank, corporation, or government agency) in possession of unclaimed property.

5.) Due Diligence: The efforts required by the holder to locate and notify the rightful owner before the property is escheated to the state.

6.) Escheatment: The process by which unclaimed property reverts to the state after a specified period of inactivity.

7.) Dormancy Period: The period during which property must remain inactive before it is considered unclaimed and eligible for escheatment.

8.) State Unclaimed Property Office: The government office responsible for administering the unclaimed property program, processing claims and handling disbursement payouts to either Claimants or Locators.

metadata.shortDescription:
Utah law requires all businesses to annually review their financial records to determine whether they are holding any funds, securities, or tangible properties that have been unclaimed for the required dormancy period, which varies based on property type, but is typically three years.

In this video and listed on the reporting overview reference sheet are five steps to report unclaimed property.

metadata.title: Unclaimed Property: Holder Reporting - Oil and Gas Companies
metadata.author: txcomptroller
metadata.shortDescription: This video provides an overview of requirements for oil and gas companies reporting unclaimed property in Texas. Unclaimed property can include expense checks, employee wage checks, miscellaneous outstanding checks and mineral proceeds that are considered abandoned by the owner. Learn more at ClaimItTexas.gov.

segments.text: Welcome to this training on how to report unclaimed property for oil and gas companies.
The oil and gas industry is one of the largest unclaimed property reporting groups in the state.
This video will guide you through the process of evaluating your procedures
and practices regarding dormant accounts and unclaimed property reporting in Texas.
What is unclaimed property?
Unclaimed property is any financial asset or intangible
personal property abandoned by the owner for periods ranging from 1 to 15 years.
Oil and gas companies might have unclaimed property to report in the form of expense checks,
employee wage checks, miscellaneous outstanding checks and royalty payments.
Items reportable as mineral proceeds include but are not limited to uncashed royalty checks,
abandoned working interests and overriding royalties.
Tangible or real property such as land or physical
assets on the lease should not be reported as unclaimed property.
Businesses that have unclaimed mineral proceeds for longer than
3 years are required to report and remit that property to the state.
Businesses should not report property as abandoned if:
One- there is documented contact with the owner either by mail, email or phone.
Two- there is owner-generated activity.
Three- or an owner has other active accounts with the business.
Businesses are required to file a report on or before July 1 of
every year for property presumed abandoned.
The property type determines the length of the abandonment period.
For example, the MI02 property type, royalties,
is considered abandoned after 3 years of inactivity while the MS01 property type,
wages, payroll or salary, is considered abandoned after 1 year of inactivity.
To determine the abandonment period, start with the last date of documented communication with the
owner, the date a check was issued or the date the funds became payable, whichever is most recent.

metadata.title: The Mechanics of Escheatment: How to Reclaim Your Abandoned Assets
metadata.author: Money Grammar
metadata.shortDescription:
Millions of dollars in dormant financial accounts are transferred to state custody annually because owners lose track of them.

In this episode, you will learn:
- The Reality of Abandoned Accounts
- The Legal Mechanism of Escheatment
- How the Custodial System Works
- Navigating the Recovery Process
- Practical Steps for Asset Protection

Sources:
USA.gov, How to find unclaimed money from the government | USAGov
https://www.usa.gov/unclaimed-money

Investor.gov, Escheatment by Financial Institutions - Investor.gov
https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/escheatment

This content is for general education only and is not financial, legal, or tax advice. Verify details with the relevant institution and your own account documents.

Narration and visual production may use AI-assisted tools.

#PersonalFinance #FinancialLiteracy #MoneyGrammar

Read full article at: https://1lessproblem.com/guides/what-is-escheatment-reclaim-unclaimed-money

segments.text: Many citizens leave their financial
assets inactive, which can lead to the
state taking custody of these assets
through a legal process called
escheatment. This transfer occurs after
an account remains inactive for a
specific time frame known as a dormancy
period, which is often around 5 years.
In this episode, we will examine how
these abandoned assets are transferred,
how the custodial system works, and how
you can recover your property. Chapter
1, the reality of abandoned accounts.
When we manage our personal finances, we
focus on active tasks like budgeting,
paying bills, and investing for the
future. However, a significant amount of
capital sits completely inactive in
accounts that have been forgotten or
abandoned by their rightful owners.
These assets can take many forms,
including inactive savings and checking
accounts, uncashed payroll checks,
forgotten security deposits, and unpaid
life insurance policies. Over time, if
there is no owner-generated activity on
these accounts, financial institutions
cannot simply keep the funds for
themselves. Instead, they're legally
required to report and transfer these
assets to state governments. This
process is highly structured and
governed by specific legal frameworks
designed to protect consumers. State
governments hold most unclaimed money,
including bank accounts, insurance
policies, and uncashed checks. This
means that if you have an old bank
account from a state where you used to
live, or an uncashed check from a
previous employer, that money is likely
sitting in a state-managed custodial
account waiting for you to claim it.
Understanding how these assets
transition from active accounts to state
custody is the first step in ensuring
that your hard-earned assets do not
remain idle. Many people do not realize
how easily an account can fall into
inactivity. A simple move to a new
address, a change of email, or the
passing of a relative can result in
financial accounts losing connection
with their owners. When communication
breaks down, the clock begins to tick on
the account's active status. This is not
a rare occurrence. Millions of dollars
are transferred to state custody
annually because of simple
administrative oversights. By
understanding the scope of this issue,
you can better appreciate why these
consumer protection laws exist and how
they serve to safeguard your financial
interests over the long term. Chapter
two, the legal mechanism of escheatment.
To understand how these assets are
managed, we must look at the legal
concept of escheatment. Escheatment is
the process by which unclaimed or
abandoned property is transferred to the
custody of state government.
Historically, this concept dates back to
common law, but today it serves as a
consumer protection measure. When a
financial institution, such as a bank or
an insurance company, notices that there
has been no activity on account for an
extended duration, the account is
classified as dormant. All states have
unclaimed property programs that require
financial institutions to report and
transfer abandoned assets to the state
after a specified dormancy period, often
around 5 years. It is crucial to
understand that escheatment laws,
dormancy periods, and claiming
procedures vary by state. During the
dormancy period, the financial
institution is typically required to
make a good faith effort to contact the
account owner using the last known
address on file. This outreach often
involves sending written notices via
mail or electronic communication warning
the owner that their account is at risk
of being declared dormant. If the owner
does not respond or perform a qualifying
transaction, the institution must report
the asset to the state's unclaimed
property program. Once the report is
filed, the actual transfer of the asset
takes place. The state does not take
permanent ownership of these funds in a
way that deprives you of your rights.
Instead, the state becomes the custodial
holder of the asset. This means the
state holds the property in perpetuity
or until the rightful owner or their
legal heir step forward to make claim.
This custodial relationship is a vital
distinction because it ensures that the
financial institution cannot simply
absorb your funds as profit. It keeps
the funds safe under government
oversight until they could be reunited
with their rightful owner. Chapter 3,
how the custodial system works. Once the
state receives the escheats assets, it
places them into a centralized unclaimed
property fund. State governments hold
most unclaimed money, including bank
accounts, insurance policies, and

metadata.title: MissingMoney.com Scam or Legit? Here's the Answer.
metadata.author: Jordan Liles
metadata.shortDescription:
People are searching around to find out if a missing money website called MissingMoney.com is a scam or legit, and they want to see reviews. Well, my findings about MissingMoney com are that the website is indeed legitimate. Here's how I know. MissingMoney.com is being searched for with the words scam and legit as well as the word reviews, but the good news is that if you do a search of Google News for the website, you'll find plenty of favorable coverage from the likes of Good Morning America, CNET, and other publications that have spoken to the legitimacy of the missing money website.

According to the MissingMoney.com website, which is legit and is not a scam, "MissingMoney.com is the only website endorsed by States and Provinces working together to reunite you with your lost funds." The website also says it's the only national site endorsed by the National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators (NAUPA) and the National Association of State Treasurers (NAST).

I noticed in September 2023 that people were looking around for MissingMoney.com for the words scam and legit. If anyone knows why, please let me know in the comments down below.

When I first looked to find out if MissingMoney.com was a scam or legit, I looked up my own name and noticed a lot of similarly-named people had outstanding payments they could claim from medical clinics, insurance companies, Costco, and others.

I hope you found this video helpful. I also hope you find some missing money. Please like my video and hit the heart-shaped button to the right of the like button. That heart-shaped button is a thanks button. I would appreciate it. Thank you for watching.

metadata.title: Your Family Could Be Owed $10,000+ And You Don’t Even Know It | Private Investigator Explains
metadata.author: Open Book Entrepreneur
metadata.shortDescription:
Most people have no idea that the government is holding millions in unclaimed money — bank accounts, life insurance payouts, investments, tax foreclosure surplus funds, asset inheritance… sometimes sitting there for decades.
My guest Tamara Rucker, licensed Private Investigator & Asset Recovery Specialist, helps families legally claim money they already own — often from relatives who passed away many years ago.
In this episode we cover:
✅ Why states have "lost-and-found money" accounts
✅ How to check if YOU or a family member are owed money
✅ What happens when someone passes away without claiming assets
✅ How Tamara helps recover funds (and avoid scams)
✅ Real stories of families receiving life-changing payouts
Check if you’re owed money:
https://www.missingmoney.com
(or search your state Treasury’s Unclaimed Property site)
Connect With Tamara:
🌐 Website: ruckwoodrecovery.com
📺 YouTube: Ruckwood Recovery
📞 Facebook: Ruckwood Recovery
If you learn something or find money — come back and comment.
We love hearing those stories.

#UnclaimedMoney #PrivateInvestigator #FoundMoney #HiddenWealth #Inheritance #SurplusFunds #AssetRecovery #LostMoney #FamilyWealth #FinancialEducation #OpenBookEntrepreneur

metadata.title: Is the Government Holding Your Money? How to Find Unclaimed Money Free
metadata.author: Dollar Decoded
metadata.shortDescription:
Is the government holding money that belongs to you? States hold more than $70 billion in unclaimed money: forgotten bank accounts, last paychecks, security deposits and insurance money nobody collected. About 1 in 7 Americans has unclaimed money waiting. Here's how to find unclaimed money for free, step by step.

Follow Jake, Maya and Leo as they search for their lost money, and learn where to look, how to claim it, and the scam that tricks people every day.

🔎 Free official places to search:
• MissingMoney.com and Unclaimed.org (state unclaimed property programs)
• NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator (a loved one's life insurance)
• U.S. Department of Labor Retirement Savings Lost and Found (old 401(k)s and pensions)

⚠️ Never pay a fee to search for or claim your own money.

💬 Comment how much you found. I'll pin the best one!

CHAPTERS
0:00 $70 billion is waiting for its owners
0:31 Jake, Maya and Leo's stories
1:24 Where your lost money goes
2:00 How much money is out there
2:36 What counts as unclaimed money
3:09 How to search, step by step (free)
4:18 4 bonus places to check
5:48 The unclaimed money scam
6:30 How to never lose money again
7:08 What our three friends found

SOURCES
• National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators (NAUPA): unclaimed.org
• State totals for California, Texas and Ohio: NewsNation
• FY2024 returns ($4.49 billion): NAUPA, via FOX 26 Houston
• NAUPA & NAST scam advisory
• NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator: naic.org
• U.S. Department of Labor, Retirement Savings Lost and Found
• IRS: 3-year window to claim a tax refund
• U.S. Treasury: matured savings bonds; Treasury Hunt retired in 2025

Jake, Maya and Leo are illustrative examples. This video is for educational purposes only and is not financial or legal advice.

#UnclaimedMoney #PersonalFinance #MoneyTips

metadata.title: #EP46 | Lynn Hall on DC Unclaimed Property: Transforming Asset Recovery and Building Trust
metadata.author: Buried in Work
metadata.shortDescription:
Billions of dollars are sitting unclaimed—and you could be part of the story. Lynn Hall, a leading expert in DC unclaimed property, pulls back the curtain on the fascinating world of asset recovery, fraud prevention, and public engagement. If you think unclaimed funds and safe deposit boxes are just dusty old records, think again—there’s a high-stakes system working to reunite people with their assets and protect public trust. 

In this episode of Buried in Work, Lynn Hall, Manager of the Unclaimed Property Unit for the District of Columbia, shares her 36+ years of expertise in asset recovery and fraud prevention. You’ll learn how unclaimed property is tracked, how DC’s proactive outreach programs are helping citizens reclaim their money faster, and the surprising items found in safe deposit boxes. Plus, hear why public engagement is more important than ever—and how easy it is to check if you’re owed unclaimed funds!

Timestamps of Key Moments

00:00 – $9,000 found: Why checking matters
01:06 – Meet Lynn Hall & her 36-year mission
03:47 – DC’s unclaimed property revolution
05:18 – COVID, fraud & fast-tracking claims
07:14 – How DC finds you before you even search
08:58 – What actually counts as unclaimed property?
10:40 – Inside the vault: Bonds, cognac & more
15:52 – Surprising discoveries with historic value
17:31 – Weird finds: diapers, bricks & fake gold
20:02 – “I’m not rich” — why that excuse doesn’t work
25:54 – How and where to claim your money

Key Takeaways
✔️ Unclaimed property isn’t just for the wealthy—millions in DC alone are waiting to be claimed.
✔️ DC’s outreach programs proactively connect people to their unclaimed funds using smart matching tools.
✔️ Items from safe deposit boxes—like historic portraits and vintage cognac—are carefully inventoried and auctioned if unclaimed.
✔️ COVID sparked innovation but also increased fraud, leading DC to tighten verification processes and build a fraud unit.
✔️ You can search for unclaimed property online in just minutes—and claim money you didn't know was yours.

metadata.shortDescription:
What is unclaimed property?

Unclaimed property are abandoned accounts in financial institutions and companies that have had no activity generated or contact with the owner for one year or a longer period. Common forms of unclaimed property include savings or checking accounts, stocks, uncashed dividends or payroll checks, refunds, traveler's checks, trust distributions, unredeemed money orders or gift certificates (in some states), insurance payments or refunds and life insurance policies, annuities, certificates of deposit, customer overpayments, utility security deposits, mineral royalty payments, and contents of safe deposit boxes.

metadata.title: Never Cash a Check? The State Ends Up Holding It
metadata.author: Base_Rate
metadata.shortDescription:
# What Really Happens to a Check If You Never Cash It?

That check in your drawer isn't waiting for you — a legal mechanism called escheatment already moved your money without your knowledge.

This video explains what actually happens when you don't cash a check. We're talking about the specific laws that govern forgotten refunds, rebates, and old paychecks — and the surprising fact that your money doesn't disappear, even though most people think it does. The culprit isn't theft or loss. It's a century-old property law that most Americans have never heard of, combined with a notification system that quietly fails to reach people.

**The check expires, but the debt doesn't.** Under Section 4-404 of the Uniform Commercial Code, banks stop honoring checks after 180 days. A check is not a container holding your money — it's an instruction telling a bank to transfer funds. Once that instruction becomes stale-dated, the bank can refuse it without explanation. But here's the crucial part: the payer still owes you. That amount stays on their books as an outstanding liability. The money doesn't vanish. The instruction does.

**States have a legal obligation to take custody of it.** Every state has an unclaimed property law, most based on uniform acts dating back to 1954. Once a check sits uncashed past the dormancy period — typically one to five years depending on the state — the payer must make a good-faith effort to contact you, usually by letter. If you don't respond, they're legally required to file a report with the state and remit the funds. This isn't voluntary. Non-compliance carries penalties. The state then holds the money indefinitely, in trust, until you claim it. This transfer is called escheatment, and it has governed abandoned assets in America for over a century.

**The numbers are staggering.** New York's State Comptroller has been processing escheatment claims since 1943. As of 2024, the office held over $19 billion in unclaimed property — some entries dating to the 1950s. Nationally, the National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators reported that states collectively held roughly $70 billion as of 2023. That money belongs to people. It's not lost or forfeited. It's sitting in a database, waiting.

**You can find your money for free.** Search "unclaimed property" plus any state or city where you've lived or worked. The search is free and run by the states themselves. The money doesn't expire in most jurisdictions. The gap between "the state has your money" and "you know the state has your money" is where most of it stays.

If you've ever wondered where old paychecks, refunds, or security deposits go, the answer is neither lost nor kept by the payer. It's held by your state, right now, under your name. Search your states today — you might be surprised what you find.

Subscribe to Base Rate for more data-driven breakdowns of how systems actually work, and let us know in the comments: have you ever found unclaimed money?

03:35 Where Your Money Goes

forgotten retirement funds from companies that vanished decades
ago.
Money that belongs to everyday workers who assume
that cash is gone forever.
People assume that if a bank, an old
job, or a government office owes them a
payment, someone will track them down and hand
them a check.
But when you move to a new apartment,
switch jobs, or simply change your email address,
companies lose contact with you.
Under state and federal laws, if financial property
sits untouched for a certain period, the company
cannot legally keep it.
They are forced to hand it over to
government custody, where it sits quietly in massive
databases until the rightful owner files a claim.
The first and most comprehensive place to check
is the multi-state database run in partnership

This system pulls records from nearly every state

When utility companies owe you an old security

mails a final paycheck to an outdated address,
that cash gets forwarded here.
Searching your name takes less than two minutes,

changed your last name, you need to check
every variation.

time when accounts get transferred.

You probably assume that if an official agency
has a file on you, your name is
spelled right.
In reality, state treasuries hold millions of dollars
under misspelled names, inverted first and last names,

If your name is Jonathan, someone at an
old utility company might have logged you as
John, or misspelled your street name, severing the
link to your identity completely.
A single missed letter can leave a $500
deposit sitting in state custody indefinitely.
If you lived in an apartment years ago
and never received your initial security deposit back,
searching your former state database might bring it
straight to light.
But state portals are only one piece of
the puzzle.
They do not hold federal assets, which is
why millions of people search a state registry,
find zero results, and assume they have nothing
coming.
The second official registry handles something far more
specific— unpaid wages through the United States Department
of Labor.
Their workers' owed wages system exists specifically because
companies get investigated, audited, or sued for wage
violations.
If an employer underpaid overtime, illegally withheld tips,
or failed to pay minimum wage, the federal
government recovers that money directly.
If the company cannot locate you because you
moved or changed your phone number, the Department
of Labor keeps that recovered back pay in
this database for up to three years before
transferring it to the Treasury.
Think about the last time you left an
hourly job or worked for a retail chain
that went through restructuring.
If an investigation wrapped up two years after
you quit, an investigator might have collected hundreds
of dollars on your behalf with no working
address to deliver it to.
You simply enter the name of your former
employer and your own name to see if
back pay is waiting.
The third database covers a completely different type
of money— the Pension Benefit Guarantee Corporation, known
as the PBGC.
When private companies shut down, go bankrupt, or
terminate their defined benefit pension plans, the federal
government steps in through this agency to protect
worker benefits.
If an employee worked at a manufacturing plant,
an airline, or a retail conglomerate for five
years in the 1990s and then left, they
might completely forget they earned a vested pension.
Decades later, the company is bankrupt.
The original office is gone, but the PBGC
still holds the retirement account.
This is where the second major twist hits.
Most people believe that if a company goes
out of business, whatever retirement money was tied
to their old internal pension disappears with it.
But federal insurance laws mean the government steps
in to pay those benefits, often for decades.
If you have older relatives, parents, or grandparents
who worked for legacy American corporations that no
longer exist, their names could easily be attached
to tens of thousands of dollars in guaranteed
monthly benefits that nobody has ever collected.
If you like finding useful digital tools and
hidden systems most people never hear about, hit
subscribe.
You will probably want the next one too.
The fourth official registry is Treasury Hunt, operated
directly by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service
under the Department of the Treasury.
This system tracks billions of dollars in matured,
uncashed United States savings bonds.
For generations, grandparents bought paper Series E or
Series EE bonds as baby gifts or graduation
presents.
Those paper certificates frequently got lost in attics,
destroyed in house moves, or forgotten inside old
lockboxes.
Savings bonds earn interest for up to 30
years.
Once they hit that 30-year mark, they
stop earning interest entirely.
They just sit there losing purchasing power to
inflation.
Treasury Hunt allows you to enter a social
security number or bond details to locate securities
that reached final maturity without ever being redeemed.
If someone bought a bond in your name
when you were born, the Treasury could be
holding the proceeds right now, completely untouched.
The fifth registry takes us into the housing
market, the Department of Housing and Urban Development,
or HUD.
If you have ever purchased a home with
an FHA-backed mortgage, you paid upfront or
monthly mortgage insurance premiums.
When an FHA loan is paid off early,
whether through refinancing into a conventional mortgage or
selling the house, borrowers are frequently entitled to
a partial refund of their insurance premium.
HUD maintains an entire searchable database of unclaimed
insurance refunds and share payments.
Homeowners frequently refinance their property through a new
lender, move away, and never realize that HUD
issued a premium refund check that went back
to the original title company or bounced off
an old mailing address.
If you refinanced an FHA loan any time
in the past 15 years, your name could
be sitting on that list with a check
attached.
Now, remember the question from the beginning about
how an entire retirement fund could just sit
in government hands without anyone reaching out.
Here is why that happens.
Federal agencies are not private investigators.
They do not run credit checks or hire
skip tracers to hunt down account owners.
Their legal mandate is simply to hold the
assets, protect them from fraud, and maintain a
public portal where citizens can claim what is
legally theirs.
The burden of discovery rests entirely on you.
The surprising part is what happens when a
bank itself goes under.
That brings us to our sixth database, the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, or FDIC, unclaimed funds
locator.
When a bank fails, the FDIC steps in
to protect depositors and liquidate the institution.
In that chaotic shuffle, customer funds occasionally go
unclaimed, ranging from forgotten safety deposit box contents
to cashier checks, certificates of deposit, and dividend
payouts that were never cashed.
The FDIC keeps an active registry of unclaimed
funds from closed financial institutions.
If you held an account at a regional
bank or credit union that was acquired, restructured,
or shuttered after a financial downturn, those residual
balances do not vanish into the ether.
They get catalogued under the failed bank records.
The seventh official database covers an area most
people never consider.
The United States Bankruptcy Court's unclaimed funds locator.
If you were ever a creditor, a client,
a vendor, or even an employee of an
individual or business that filed for Chapter 7,
11, or 13 bankruptcy, the court-appointed trustee
may have distributed funds to pay debts.
If the court mailed a distribution check to
an old address and the envelope was returned
as undeliverable, the bankruptcy clerk deposits that cash
into the court registry.
The twist here is that you do not
have to be a big commercial bank to
be owed money from a bankruptcy proceeding.
You could have been an everyday customer waiting
on a refund from a travel agency that
folded, an independent contractor owed an invoice from
a failed startup, or a tenant whose former
landlord filed for corporate restructuring.
Those distribution checks sit in federal court accounts
across individual districts until claimed.
None of these seven registries charge fees to
search, and none of them take a percentage
cut of your payout.
If you ever encounter a third-party service
asking for upfront cash or demanding a 20
% locator fee to unlock your assets, you
are paying someone for work you can do
yourself in five minutes on an official government
website.
When you sit down to search these registries
tonight, whose name are you going to look
up first?
Your own?
Your parents?
Or an old family member?
Simple explanations.
Useful information.
No fluff.
I'm This Guy Knows Tech.
Subscribe for more digital cheat codes.
And I'll see you in the next one.

Homeowners frequently refinance their property through a new lender, move away, and never realize that HUD issued a premium refund check that went back to the original title company or bounced off an old mailing address. If you refinanced an FHA loan any time in the past 15 years, your name could be sitting on that list with a check attached. Now, remember the question from the beginning about how an entire retirement fund could just sit in government hands without anyone reaching out. Here is why that happens. Federal agencies are not private investigators. They do not run credit checks or hire skip tracers to hunt down account owners. Their legal mandate is simply to hold the assets, protect them from fraud, and maintain a public portal where citizens can claim what is legally theirs. The burden of discovery rests entirely on you. The surprising part is what happens when a bank itself goes under. That brings us to our sixth database, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, or FDIC, unclaimed funds locator. When a bank fails, the FDIC steps in to protect depositors and liquidate the institution. In that chaotic shuffle, customer funds occasionally go unclaimed, ranging from forgotten safety deposit box contents to cashier checks, certificates of deposit, and dividend payouts that were never cashed. The FDIC keeps an active registry of unclaimed funds from closed financial institutions. If you held an account at a regional bank or credit union that was acquired, restructured, or shuttered after a financial downturn, those residual balances do not vanish into the ether. They get catalogued under the failed bank records. The seventh official database covers an area most people never consider. The United States Bankruptcy Court's unclaimed funds locator. If you were ever a creditor, a client, a vendor, or even an employee of an individual or business that filed for Chapter 7, 11, or 13 bankruptcy, the court-appointed trustee may have distributed funds to pay debts. If the court mailed a distribution check to an old address and the envelope was returned as undeliverable, the bankruptcy clerk deposits that cash into the court registry. The twist here is that you do not have to be a big commercial bank to be owed money from a bankruptcy proceeding. You could have been an everyday customer waiting on a refund from a travel agency that folded, an independent contractor owed an invoice from a failed startup, or a tenant whose former landlord filed for corporate restructuring. Those distribution checks sit in federal court accounts across individual districts until claimed. None of these seven registries charge fees to search, and none of them take a percentage cut of your payout. If you ever encounter a third-party service asking for upfront cash or demanding a 20 % locator fee to unlock your assets, you are paying someone for work you can do yourself in five minutes on an official government website. When you sit down to search these registries tonight, whose name are you going to look up first? Your own? Your parents? Or an old family member? Simple explanations. Useful information. No fluff. I'm This Guy Knows Tech. Subscribe for more digital cheat codes. And I'll see you in the next one.

Delaware has about a million residents, and last fiscal year it booked $554 million from unclaimed money: forgotten refunds, uncashed paychecks, old deposits, and gift card balances nobody used. Here's how a 1965 Supreme Court tiebreaker turned the home of two-thirds of the Fortune 500 into the default destination for America's lost money.
Roughly 1 in 7 Americans has unclaimed property waiting somewhere. 
In this video:
• What unclaimed property and "escheat" actually mean
• The Texas v. New Jersey rule that sends address-less money to Delaware
• Delaware's $554M unclaimed property line item, and the $426M left after refunds
• The 22-year audit a federal judge called "a game of 'gotcha'"
• Delaware's 9–0 Supreme Court loss over MoneyGram checks and the $190M+ settlement
• What happens to unused gift cards: breakage, Starbucks' $1.75B balance, and the Ohio subsidiary strategy

Learn how unclaimed property works and how businesses must report forgotten funds to the state. Discover your rights to these assets.

This video explains the legal process behind unclaimed property and why companies are required to hand over funds they cannot return to rightful owners. If you are curious about how states manage these assets, this guide breaks down the reporting requirements and the auditing process that determines who holds the money.

We examine the specific regulations surrounding unclaimed money, including the complexities of the tiebreaker rule. You will learn how different jurisdictions, such as Ohio, handle cases where they do not accept certain funds. Understanding these state regulations helps you clarify whether you have assets waiting to be claimed.

Finally, we discuss the broader implications of how businesses track and report forgotten accounts. By following this process, you gain insight into why property ends up in state custody and what steps are involved in the recovery path. Knowing these rules ensures you are informed about the financial landscape regarding missing accounts.

Subscribe for weekly financial breakdowns and comment below if you want to learn more about how to search for forgotten assets in your state.

you'll probably never collect. A refund
mailed to an old address, a last
paycheck from a job you left, a deposit
on an apartment you moved out of years
ago. You're not unusual. Roughly one in
seven Americans has unclaimed money or
property sitting somewhere. That money
doesn't just vanish. After enough
silence, the business holding it has to
hand it over to a state. Which state?
That's where this gets strange. Delaware
has about a million people, and last
fiscal year it booked $554 million from
unclaimed property. That's not from
tourists, and it's not a tax on its own
residents. It comes from a 1965 Supreme
Court tiebreaker. If a company doesn't
know your address, your money goes to
the state where the company is
incorporated, and two-thirds of the
Fortune 500 are incorporated in
Delaware. So let's follow the money
nobody's looking for.
[music]
First, some vocabulary. When a business
owes you money and you go quiet, no
cashing, no logging in, no reply to
letters, a clock starts. That's the
dormancy period. When it runs out, the
business, which the law calls the
holder, has to report the money and turn
it over to the state. That handoff has
an old name. Escheat. [music] On paper,
states don't own this money. They hold
it as custodians, and you can still file
a claim. But first, somebody has to
decide which state gets to hold it. In
the early 1960s, three states fought
over the same pile of unclaimed debts
owed by an oil company, Sun Oil. Texas
said the property belonged in Texas. New
Jersey said Sun Oil was incorporated in
New Jersey, so the money was New
Jersey's. In 1965, the Supreme Court
settled it with two rules. Rule one, the
money goes to the state of the owner's
last known address [snorts] as shown in
the company's records. Rule two is the
backup. If there's no address on file,
the money goes to the state where the
company is incorporated. That sounds
tidy, but think about who the backup
rule rewards. Companies lose addresses
all the time. A check with no address
attached, a payment never matched a
customer. Every one of those falls
through to rule two. And for most of
corporate America, rule two points to
one place. Two thirds of the Fortune 500
are Delaware corporations. were 81% of
the US-based companies that went public
in 2024. More than two million legal
entities call Delaware home on paper.
None of them need an office there. They
just need to be incorporated there. And
that makes Delaware the default
destination for a lot of America's lost
money that has no address attached.
So let's open Delaware's own books. In
fiscal year 2025, Delaware's personal
income tax brought in about $2.7
billion.
The franchise tax, the annual fee
companies pay to stay incorporated
there, brought in about 1.3 billion.
Right behind those two came [music]
unclaimed property, 554 million. And
this isn't new. Back in 2007, about $365
million in unclaimed property went into
Delaware's general fund. When a federal
judge later examined the program, he
cited the state's own documents
describing that money as a vital element
of its operating budget. Delaware has
about 1.06 million residents. Divide
that 554 million across everyone in the
state and you get roughly $523 a person.
To be clear, Delawareans aren't paying
it. That's the point. The money comes in
from holders whose customers live
everywhere. For scale, look at Texas. On
its own, Texas would rank as roughly the
ninth largest economy on earth. In
fiscal 2021, its unclaimed property fund
took in about $793 million gross.
Delaware pulls in a figure in the same
league with a sliver of the people. That
554 million is the gross figure and some
of it goes back out. The same year,
Delaware recorded $128 million in
refunds paid out on claims. That leaves
about 426 million net. Here's the
structural part. In Delaware, unclaimed
money that nobody claims flows into the
general fund and helps pay for the same
things taxes do. Nationally, states do
give a lot back. $4.49 billion returned
to owners in fiscal 2024, but an older
analysis from the state's own
association found they return only about
half as much as they take in. So every
unclaimed property program runs on a
quiet tension. Its official job is
reuniting people with their money, but
the budget looks better when people
don't show up. Delaware has the same
incentive as everyone else, just with a
lot more money riding on it. And when a
budget leans on a revenue stream,
someone goes looking for more of it.
Unclaimed property doesn't only show up
when companies report it on their own.
States audit, and Delaware brought in
private contract auditors to do it. The
best known is a firm called Kelmar
Associates, [music] which was reportedly
paid somewhere between $25 and $50
million a year. Here's how one of those
audits went. Temple Inland was a
manufacturer incorporated in Delaware
with most of its operations outside the
state. In 2008, Delaware's auditors
opened an audit that reached back 22
years from 1986 through 2007. Most
companies don't keep records that far
back, and Temple Inland had thrown its
old ones out. So the auditors estimated.
They took the unclaimed property they
found in recent years, used it to infer
what must have existed in the years with
no records, and then assessed the
company for it. In 2016, a federal judge
reviewed the whole process. His verdict,
Delaware had engaged in a game of gotcha
that shocks the conscience. The case
settled before any remedy was decided,
but it put the whole machine under a
spotlight. The bigger fight was still to
come, and this time it was with other
[music] states. MoneyGram sells official
checks through banks. When those checks
go uncashed, there's often no address
for the buyer. So for years, MoneyGram
sent that money to its state of
incorporation, Delaware, under Rule 2.
Pennsylvania and Wisconsin objected, and
eventually 30 states lined up against
Delaware. Their argument, a federal law,
the Federal Disposition Act, sends this
kind of money to the state where each
check was bought. In February 2023, the
Supreme Court agreed with them 9 to 0.
It was the court's first unclaimed
property ruling in about 30 years. In
2024, Delaware settled. More than $190
million in unclaimed property went to
the other states, including over $102
million transferred by Delaware itself.
The backup rule is still the law, but
the ruling drew a line. When federal law
says the money follows the purchase, the
tiebreaker doesn't apply. So far, this
is all been checks and payments, but
there's one kind of forgotten money
that's probably in your kitchen drawer
right now, and it plays by different
rules.
In a 2024 bank rate survey, 43% of US
adults said they had at least one unused
gift card, voucher, or store credit. The
average balance was $244,
up from $116 just 3 years earlier. Bank
rate puts the national total at about
$27 billion. For the company, a gift
card is a great deal. You pay today,
they hand over the coffee or the sweater
later or never. Bank rate's analyst says
Walmart and Starbucks each carry more
than a billion dollars in unused gift
cards on their books. Starbucks's own
filing shows how big that pile can get.
At the end of its 2025 fiscal year, it
was holding $1.75 billion in stored
value card balances and loyalty rewards
that customers had paid for or earned,
but not yet used. On the balance sheet,
that's a liability, money it owes you in
coffee. When a balance looks like it
will never be used, the company can
eventually count it as revenue.
Accountants call this breakage, and
Starbucks reports it on the same line as
the cards customers actually redeemed,
which raises the obvious question.
Shouldn't that money go to the state
instead? [music]
It depends on where the card's issuer is
legally based. Around 37 states either
exempt gift cards from unclaimed
property law or simply don't require
them to be turned over. Delaware is one
of the states that does require it. So a
common strategy is to set up a separate
subsidiary in a state that exempts gift
cards, like Ohio, Virginia, or Florida,
and have that subsidiary issue the
cards. Now run the tiebreaker. A gift
card has no owner address, so the money
goes to the issuer's state, and that
state doesn't take gift card balances.
The money has nowhere to go, so it stays
with the company. Delaware has pushed
back. Marathon and Speedway, both
Delaware corporations, ran their gift
cards through subsidiaries based in
Ohio. Delaware's auditors expanded their
audit to cover those cards anyway, and a
federal appeals court let that audit
move forward. For you, there are at
least two floors. [music]
Under federal law since 2010, gift card
money generally can't expire for at
least 5 years, and a store can't start
charging inactivity fees until a card
has gone unused for at least a year. So
here's the full receipt, the refund you
forgot, the paycheck you never cashed,
the gift card in the drawer. Each one
ends up in one of three places, [music]
back with you, in a state budget, or on
a company's income statement. Which one
it is depends less on where you live and
more on a rule from 1965 and where a
company chose to file its paperwork.
Roughly one in seven of us has something
waiting. Every state runs an unclaimed
property program, and the state's own
association points people to one place
to search, missingmoney.com.
That's what they don't show you. The
money you forget doesn't disappear.
Somebody else just gets to count it.

metadata.title: Unclaimed Property in Tennessee: Understanding Audits, Compliance, and Negative Reports
metadata.author: TNTreasury
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn about Unclaimed Property audits, compliance and negative reports in this instructional video, part of an Unclaimed Property Holder Video Series by the Tennessee Department of Treasury, Division of Unclaimed Property.

You can access this video with a visual description by using this link: https://youtu.be/GABm_HFIThI

segments.text: Unclaimed Property: Understanding Audits, Compliance and Negative Reports
Let's start by talking about the Unclaimed Property
Audit and Compliance Disclosure Agreement program.
The Tennessee Department of Treasury conducts
audits of the books and records of companies throughout the country
to determine if they're in compliance with unclaimed property statutes.
Things that may prompt an audit include: a business's lack of unclaimed property reporting history,
a complaint against a business such as a whistleblower,
a randomly selected sample of companies,
or through a multi-state audit.
One way holders can avoid an audit is to voluntarily file a negative report with the State.
The purpose of a negative report is to inform the Unclaimed Property Division that after your
due diligence efforts, you do not have any property to report.
Negative reports are not required.
However, if you choose to submit a negative report, it can only be submitted through the online portal: ReportItTN.
If a business holding unclaimed property that's beyond the dormancy period
becomes aware of the legal requirement to report it to the State,
the business can voluntarily choose to enter into a compliance disclosure agreement with the state.
So what is the CDA program?
This agreement states that the holder will come into compliance
with unclaimed property statutes within a certain period,
allowing the holder to avoid a potential audit and penalty fees.
How does a holder qualify for the CDA program?
A business cannot be currently under audit by the state
at the time it chooses to sign the compliance Disclosure agreement.
The holder must present a proposal of Reporting Method worksheet
describing in detail how the holder's unclaimed property liability will be determined.
This process avoids the Unclaimed Property Division
physically reviewing a company's unclaimed property records.
A business must send to the State its current written procedures
regarding its handling of unclaimed property.
A copy of the CDA is available on our website: Treasury.TN.gov.
Penalties are avoided when a holder discloses unclaimed property upfront through the CDA program.
Negligent failure to report, deliver or remit unclaimed property to the State
results in a $200 per day penalty fine, with a maximum of $5,000.
Willful failure to meet holder duties results in a $1,000 per day penalty, up to a $25,000 maximum,
plus 25% of the value of the property for which the holder had a duty to report.

metadata.title: SALT: Top 5 Mistakes Companies Make Evaluating Their Unclaimed Property Exposure.
metadata.author: SimekScott LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Unclaimed property can be easily overlooked and even small mistakes identifying, reporting or managing your obligations can create unnecessary exposure. in this discussion, SimekScott dissects the top 5 mistakes companies commonly make when evaluating their unclaimed property exposure. 

We cover practical considerations that can help companies identify potential exposure, avoid reporting and compliance pitfalls, identify internal processes that create risk and create a practical approach to managing unclaimed property. 

Whether your company is just beginning to evaluate its obligations or already has an established process, SimekScott provides practical insights to help avoid the most common traps.

metadata.title: What Is Escheatable in Oil & Gas? Unclaimed Property Explained
metadata.author: PakEnergy
metadata.shortDescription:
Uncashed royalty checks, AP funds sitting in suspense, shifting state rules — is your unclaimed property reporting a risk hiding in plain sight?

For energy companies with thousands of interest owners and extensive supply chains, unclaimed property is one of the most frustrating compliance challenges there is. In this webinar, PakEnergy accounting experts Nikki Naylor and Joel Cox break down what you need to know to navigate reporting season and de-risk escheat compliance.

You'll learn:
- What qualifies as escheatable, and the types of unclaimed property common in oil & gas
- How to keep up with legislative and reporting changes, including the shift from NAUPA II to NAUPA III and uneven RUUPA adoption across states
- How to mitigate hidden unclaimed property risk from mergers and acquisitions
- How Voluntary Disclosure Agreement (VDA) programs can minimize penalties and interest
- How dedicated unclaimed property tools with owner contact tracking and filing rules simplify reporting

Whether you're preparing for your next filing deadline or cleaning up after an acquisition, you'll come away with actionable steps to save time, reduce stress, and protect your business from costly risk.

About the Speakers
Nikki Naylor is Product Manager, Accounting at PakEnergy. Joel Cox is an Account Executive, Mid-Market at PakEnergy.

👉 Schedule a demo: https://pakenergy.com/schedule-demo
📚 Explore additional resources: https://pakenergy.com/resources

About PakEnergy
PakEnergy, LLC (A Delaware LLC) is redefining how energy companies operate with a unified software platform that unlocks value across the energy lifecycle. Its audit-ready accounting suite gives energy teams the controls, compliance, and clear financial visibility to protect the bottom line — backed by intelligent automation and advanced analytics that extend across land, production, and the full operation. Headquartered in Texas, PakEnergy proudly supports over 2,300 customers with a team of seasoned professionals from the energy and technology sectors, each committed to helping clients thrive in a fast-changing industry.

metadata.title: How to Automate Unclaimed Property Workflows in Oil & Gas
metadata.author: PakEnergy
metadata.shortDescription:
Tracking owners, running due diligence, untangling dormancy and filing rules — what if your unclaimed property process ran itself?

If you're an oil & gas accounting pro frustrated by the complexity of unclaimed property management, this session is for you. Unclaimed property compliance expert Nikki Naylor and co-host Joel Cox return with a hands-on look at how purpose-built software handles each step of the escheat process — from owner tracking to filing.

In this webinar, you'll get:
- Clear definitions for complex escheat terminology
- A quick recap of the key unclaimed property challenges facing oil & gas companies
- Live demos of how PakEnergy's Unclaimed Property module tracks owners, manages due diligence, and applies dormancy and filing rules automatically

Whether you're managing escheat in spreadsheets today or evaluating a better way, you'll see exactly what an automated unclaimed property workflow looks like in action.

About the Speakers
Nikki Naylor is Product Manager, Accounting at PakEnergy and an unclaimed property compliance expert. Joel Cox is an Account Executive, Mid-Market at PakEnergy.

👉 Schedule a demo: https://pakenergy.com/schedule-demo
📚 Explore additional resources: https://pakenergy.com/resources

About PakEnergy
PakEnergy, LLC (A Delaware LLC) is redefining how energy companies operate with a unified software platform that unlocks value across the energy lifecycle. Its audit-ready accounting suite gives energy teams the controls, compliance, and clear financial visibility to protect the bottom line — backed by intelligent automation and advanced analytics that extend across land, production, and the full operation. Headquartered in Texas, PakEnergy proudly supports over 2,300 customers with a team of seasoned professionals from the energy and technology sectors, each committed to helping clients thrive in a fast-changing industry.

metadata.author: Broadstreet Radio

Step-by-step guide to recovering your unclaimed dividends in the Nigerian capital market.

Many investors are unaware that they may have unpaid or unclaimed dividends sitting in their name without realizing it. In this video, you’ll learn a simple and practical process to help you identify, verify, and recover your unclaimed dividends safely.

We break it down in a clear, beginner-friendly way so you can take action immediately and avoid leaving your money unclaimed.

📌 In this video, you will learn:

What unclaimed dividends are
Why dividends go unclaimed
How to check if you have unclaimed dividends
Step-by-step process to recover them
Important tips to avoid future issues

Take control of your investments and ensure your money is working for you.

💬 Have you ever checked if you have unclaimed dividends? Let us know in the comments.

#UnclaimedDividends #InvestingNigeria #StockMarketNigeria #financialeducation   #ngx   #wealthbuilding   #capitalmarkets   #personalfinanceeducation

metadata.title: What happen to Unclaimed dividend amount?
metadata.author: Claim My Shares
metadata.shortDescription:
When dividends remain unclaimed by shareholders for an extended period, they typically don't just disappear. Instead, companies usually hold onto these unclaimed dividends in a separate account, often referred to as "unclaimed dividend account" or similar. These funds are still owed to the shareholders, and the company maintains responsibility for them. Companies are legally required to make efforts to locate the rightful owners of unclaimed dividends. They may send out notifications to shareholders, publish notices in newspapers, or use other means to try to reach them. If shareholders fail to claim their dividends within a specified period, the company may transfer these unclaimed funds to a separate fund or escheat them to the state government, depending on local regulations. It's essential for shareholders to keep their contact information updated with the company to ensure they receive dividends and other communications.

Many Nigerians and their parents have forgotten shares and unclaimed dividends worth thousands — even millions — of naira.

In this video, I explain STEP-BY-STEP how to: ✅ Recover lost share certificates
✅ Trace forgotten investments
✅ Find your CHN number
✅ Contact registrars
✅ Consolidate shares digitally
✅ Reactivate unclaimed dividends

Learn how to safely find unclaimed money that's owed to you and claim it through legitimate and free state-sanctioned unclaimed money and property registries.

According to the National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators, about 1 in 10 people have unclaimed property, which means accounts that have had no activity or contact with the owner for over a year.

Both of these registries you can search on your own for FREE.

Most states participate in this site:
http://www.missingmoney.com/
 
You can also check out this one:
http://www.unclaimed.org/

=======================================
Here are some other free and legit government websites sites you might want use to check for unclaimed money or unclaimed property:

Department of Treasury Unclaimed Money
https://fiscal.treasury.gov/unclaimed-assets.html

California State Controller's Office - Unclaimed Property
https://www.sco.ca.gov/upd_msg.html

Unclaimed Money from the U.S. Government
https://www.usa.gov/unclaimed-money

Don’t click on anything that isn’t a government website or endorsed by the government. In some cases that endorsement can be fishy, so always validate!

segments.text: Did you know that today there’s about $33 BILLION dollars in unclaimed money,
just hanging out in state treasuries and other agencies waiting to be claimed?
But there are also a lot of shenanigans on the
internet claiming to help you find free or unclaimed money.
So how do you check to see if you have any unclaimed money?
Is this really a thing? And are unclaimed money sites legit?
By the way, hello and WELCOME!
I’m Penelope Jane Smith, and I’m here to break it down for you…
My intention with this channel is to give you the financial education you never got at home or in
school growing up so you can set yourself up to be financially secure for the rest of your life.
Now let’s tap the “Like” button for the YouTube
algorithm and dive into the world of unclaimed money…
So as I mentioned, there’s about $33 billion dollars in unclaimed money in the U.S. right now.
In this video, I’m going to use the term “unclaimed money.”
But it can also be called “unclaimed funds” or “missing money” or “unclaimed property.”
And also as I mentioned, you might see messages or sites on the internet claiming
to help you find free or unclaimed money so you want to be cautious.
For example, some messages will urge you to immediately call or fax a
number in the Caribbean, which doesn’t require an international code to dial,
but you’ll be charged very high rates for the call.
Other people will charge you unnecessary fees or simply try
to gather your personal information in order to commit identity theft.
Or you might get an official-looking email asking you to fill in your information on a website.
You don’t want to enter your info into a suspicious looking website,
and you definitely don’t want to send them money!
Keep in mind that unclaimed prosperity offices don’t reach out to people to
let them know they have unclaimed money. This might vary from country to country,
but to my knowledge, in the U.S., they don’t reach out.
And you NEVER have to pay to reclaim your money!!!
If someone contacts you needing some money to “unlock” some unclaimed money or “register”
to see some unclaimed money, just… run away. Delete, block, get out of there.
ALL that said, there ARE legitimate,
state-sanctioned unclaimed property registries that you can search on your own for FREE.
There’s a group called the National Association of Unclaimed Property
Administrators, and they say that about 1 in 10 people have unclaimed property,
which means accounts that have had no activity or contact with the owner for over a year.
After a certain period of time, called the “dormancy period,” if there’s no
activity or contact, the money or property officially becomes “unclaimed” and by law,
it has to be turned over to the state. Some common examples include savings or
checking accounts, stocks, uncashed dividends or payroll checks, refunds, and traveler's checks.
Then there’s trust distributions, unredeemed money orders or gift certificates (in some states),
insurance payments or refunds and life insurance policies.
Plus, there’s annuities, certificates of deposit, customer overpayments, utility security deposits,
mineral royalty payments, and even contents of safe deposit boxes.
Companies are legally required to send funds from lost accounts to the state of
the owner's last known address. So do a search for each of the states that you’ve lived in.
Also, claims can often be made in perpetuity, even by heirs.
This is how I helped my aunt find some unclaimed
money that my grandma had left behind when she died.
I found some specific stories that I love, because I love unexpected checks!
Here are a couple of fun stories that my team shared with me...
Bill found $200 in a closed bank account that he
didn’t even remember he had - his son actually remembered and looked it up!
And Mike found an old paycheck that he hadn’t claimed after he quit a job and moved. It took
him about 30 minutes to sign up on the site and get verified and got over a thousand dollars,
which he put straight towards paying off his credit card debt.
This actually highlights one of the main reasons money goes unclaimed - the Post
Office will only forward mail for a short time if you move and if an
organization wants to find you, the mail might go undelivered!
So how do you check to see if you have any unclaimed money?
Both of these sites are great for helping you find unclaimed money.
Most states participate in this site: http://www.missingmoney.com/
You can also check out this one: http://www.unclaimed.org/
I’ve put these links in the description of this video so they’re easy for you to find.
Remember to do a search for every state you’ve lived in. And if you have family
members that have passed on, you might want to do a search for every state they’ve lived in.
And you might want to circle back every now and then, maybe once a year,
to check again. Things change over time.
Now, these tips apply specifically to people who have lived in the United States,
District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, or parts of Canada.
What if you don't live in one of those areas? Well, I don’t know the specifics in every country,
but here’s a related tip that’ll be helpful wherever you live…
Do a Google search for missing money plus the name of your state, country or province.
You should see an official government website in the top of the search results.
Don’t click on anything that isn’t a government website or
endorsed by the government. In some cases that endorsement can be fishy, so always validate!
And here’s another tip, wherever you live…
Consider contacting the various institutions that hold your money or property every year,
especially when something significant changes. Keep records of all your insurance policies,
bank names and account numbers, stock certificates, and any rent and utility deposits.
If you’ve found this helpful, please tap the “Like” button on this video, if you
haven’t already done that, because it really helps me reach more people with this message.
If you’d like to see more videos from me around personal finance,
money management, saving and investing, and financial freedom, make sure to SUBSCRIBE
to this channel and click the little bell icon so you’ll see when I make a new video.
And if you want to find out what it’ll take for you personally to become financially
free so you don’t have to depend on your business, a job, the government,
a partner, or anyone else for money, go to MyFinancialFreedomFormula.com or click the
link in the description to download your free copy of my ebook, The Financial Freedom Formula.
Thanks again for watching, and I hope you find some unexpected money!

Watch this video and learn how to search the state of Delaware unclaimed property division to find missing and abandoned property. In the last three years, over $300 million has been returned to the rightful owners. Could you be next?

There are countless property owners in the state of Delaware and across the country don't know they have property in their name. In my experience, many don't believe. The truth is I was one of them but after listening to my wife I found money.

When you submit a claim that belongs to you, you'll be given a claim number and a phone number is available in case you want to speak to someone.

Not from Delaware or want to search a few other states that you've worked, lived, have family members of history, go to https://forgottenloot.org for complete details.

Good luck,

metadata.title: Delaware Unclaimed Property VDA Invitations - April 11 2025
metadata.author: SimekScott LLC
metadata.shortDescription: The Delaware Secretary of State will issue invitations around April 11, 2025 to companies for participation in its Unclaimed Property Voluntary Disclosure Agreement (VDA) program.  Watch our update from our Managing Principal on this development in Delaware to help you stay proactive and compliant.

segments.text: Hi everyone, my name is Matt Bower,
managing principal at Simic Scott and
today I'm going to be discussing the
next round of invitations into the state
of Delaware's unclaimed property VDA
program. On April 11th, the Delaware
Secretary of State is going to be
sending out VDA invitations. If your
company receives an invitation to
participate in the state of Delaware's
unclaimed property VDA program, you have
to take action within the first 90 days
to determine whether or not you're going
to participate in the VDA program. If
you decide not to participate, just know
that you will be referred to the
Department of Finance for an unclaimed
property audit. So, a couple things that
your company needs to think about if you
receive one of these invitations. The
first thing is whether or not you've
been compliant with the laws within the
state of Delaware with respect to
unclaimed property. The second thing
you're going to want to think about is
how many of your companies are
incorporated in Delaware that have
significant operations.
Um, another thing to think about too is
not only the entities that are
incorporated in Delaware, but if you
have entities that are not incorporated
in Delaware, but have a significant
customer base, employee base, or vendor
base within the state, that may also
generate unclaimed property. The next
thing you're going to want to think
about is whether or not you feel your
staff is equipped to handle an unclaimed
property BDA project. And one way to see
that's all involved with the BDA project
would be to go out to the Secretary of
State site and view the sample work plan
and see all the different property types
and tasks that would be required to
complete the BDA program. Here at Simic
Scott, uh we help companies through the
BDA process from start to finish. We act
as the liaison between the company and
the VDA administrator and we're always
working to get the project completed
within the specified time
frame. Should you have any questions,
please reach out via the contact info
displayed in this video.
