metadata.title: The Tiny State That Lives Off Other People's Forgotten Money
metadata.author: The Explainer Point
metadata.shortDescription:
What happens to money when nobody comes back for it?
An uncashed paycheck, an abandoned bank account, an old dividend check, or forgotten shares can eventually become “unclaimed property.” But when nobody can be found, the money has to go somewhere.
In this video, we explain how America’s unclaimed-property system works, why the rules can send certain forgotten assets to Delaware, and why Delaware has become such an unusual center for this money.
The story involves old escheat laws, Supreme Court decisions, corporate registrations, MoneyGram, Temple-Inland, abandoned stock, and one surprisingly important line in a company’s records.
Most importantly, there is a strange contradiction at the center of the system:
The state can hold and use the money, but it does not actually own it.
This is a story about forgotten money, legal addresses, corporate paperwork, and the unusual economics hiding behind something most people never think about.

Delaware unclaimed money, Delaware forgotten money, unclaimed property explained, escheat explained, abandoned property, Delaware economy, Delaware corporate laws, unclaimed assets, lost money, forgotten bank accounts, uncashed checks, abandoned stock, MoneyGram Delaware, Delaware escheat, state unclaimed property, how unclaimed money works, forgotten money in America, Delaware finance, corporate registration Delaware, financial history

Delaware, unclaimed money, forgotten money, unclaimed property, escheat, escheat explained, Delaware economy, Delaware finance, lost money, abandoned money, unclaimed assets, uncashed checks, forgotten bank accounts, abandoned stock, MoneyGram, Delaware corporations, corporate law, Supreme Court, finance explained, economics explained, financial education, money explained, wealth explained, business explained

#Delaware #UnclaimedMoney #FinanceExplained #Economics #Money #UnclaimedProperty

segments.text: A state with about 1 million people
takes in hundreds of millions of dollars
every year that nobody ever meant to
give it. It is not a tax, it is not a
lottery, it is money that other people
forgot.
That one line covers more than 6% of
Delaware's operating budget. So, how
does a tiny state end up holding so much
money that belongs to someone else?
It starts with something small. A
paycheck is never cashed. A bank account
sits untouched. A stock dividend is
mailed to an old address and the
envelope comes back. The company that
owes the money cannot find the person.
Without a rule, the company would simply
keep the money. So, after a set number
of years with no contact, the law says
the company must hand it to a state.
That handover has an old name, escheat.
Every state and the District of Columbia
runs a program like this.
The word comes from medieval England.
When a tenant died with no heirs, the
land fell back to the lord. Today, the
state plays that role with one big
difference. The state is only a keeper.
The owner never loses the right to ask
for the money back.
Across America, states are holding an
estimated 70 billion dollars this way
and roughly one in seven Americans has
some of it waiting. In the 12 months
that ended in June 2024, states returned
about 4 and 1/2 billion dollars to
owners who came forward. The average
claim is about 2,000 dollars and states
do not charge a fee to search or to
claim.
But that raises a second question. If a
company in one state owes money to a
person in another state, which state
gets it? In the 1960s, the Supreme Court
had to decide. The case began with Sun
Oil, which owed small debts to many
people who never cashed their checks.
Texas, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and
Florida all wanted the money. In 1965,
the court set two rules. The first rule,
the money goes to the state of the
person's last known address as written
in the company's own records. The court
liked this rule because it is simple. A
company can look at its own books and
know where to send the money. The second
rule, if there is no address on file or
that state has no law to take the money,
it goes to the state where the company
was incorporated. Now, look at Delaware.
More than 2 million business entities
are registered there and about 2/3 of
the Fortune 500 are incorporated in the
state. That is about twice as many
entities as people. Companies say they
pick Delaware for its corporate laws and
its Court of Chancery. A company can
sell in Ohio, employ workers in
California, and run its headquarters in
Texas, yet its legal home can still be
Delaware. So, when that company owes
money to someone with no address on
file, the second rule points to
Delaware.
The state did not find that money. The
company's choice of legal home sent it
there.
And Delaware takes in more than its
share compared with its size. This is
not small change for the state.
Delaware's own revenue forecasters
expect $554 million from unclaimed
property in fiscal year 2027 before
refunds.
That number is also a legal ceiling.
Lawmakers capped how much can flow into
the general budget. First at $514
million in 2013, then at $554 million in
The state has hit that cap every year
since it was created and anything above
it goes into a separate account. About
$130 million is expected to be paid back
to owners leaving roughly $424 million
for the budget. The governor even
proposed raising the cap by $60 million.
Since 1977, escheated money has gone
into the general fund and claims are
paid out of that same fund. In other
words, the state spends the money first
and pays owners back later.
No one designed it as a business model.
It is the side effect of two old court
rules and one very popular legal
address.
That is why a fight over one company
mattered so much. MoneyGram is
incorporated in Delaware. It sold
official checks all over the country,
but it did not keep good records of the
addresses of the people who were owed.
When those checks went uncashed, the
second rule sent the money to Delaware.
Pennsylvania and Wisconsin challenged
that practice and a group of 30 states
backed them.
Delaware argued that official checks are
not money orders and can be written for
much larger amounts. The states answered
that a federal law from 1974 covers
money orders and similar instruments and
it sends their unclaimed money to the
state where the instrument was bought,
not the state where the company was
incorporated. The Supreme Court
appointed a special master, a federal
appeals judge, to study the dispute. And
his report sided with the states.
Pennsylvania's treasurer warned that
Delaware could owe other states as much
as $400 million. dollars.
In February 2023, the Supreme Court
agreed with the states and it was
unanimous. It was the first major
unclaimed property ruling in about 30
years and the first majority opinion
written by Justice Ketanji Brown
Jackson.
The bill came due in 2024.
Delaware agreed to hand more than $102
million to the 30 states based on where
each check was bought. It also gave up
its claim to another $89 million that
MoneyGram had set aside during the case,
which was divided among all 50 states.
State officials said the payout would
have only a minimal effect on the budget
and Delaware's escheater said the state
was pleased to close the matter and
focus on reuniting owners with their
property. Delaware has also been
challenged on how it hunts for missing
money. In one famous case, the state's
outside auditor examined a large company
called Temple Inland over a 22-year
period. Only six years of bank records
still existed, and in them, the auditor
found one unreported payroll check for
It used that sample to estimate what was
missing in the other years, even
counting money owed to people in other
states, and the bill passed $1 million.
A federal judge said the method was so
unreasonable that it violated the
company's constitutional right to fair
treatment. The case settled, and Temple
Inland paid nothing. Delaware's finance
secretary said the state would review
its escheats rules and practices. Stock
raises a harder problem. In Delaware,
shares can be treated as abandoned after
3 years without activity, and the law
lets the state sell them and put the
proceeds into the general fund. Colette
Barf, a former Microsoft employee in
South Africa, sued in 2024.
Her lawsuit says her Microsoft shares
were sent to Delaware in 2015 after a
letter was mailed to her address in
South Africa, and then sold for nearly
She says she learned about it only in
By the time she sued, the same shares
would have been worth almost $2 million.
The state says it acted lawfully under
its own law. Her case shows a gap. The
owner never loses the right to claim,
but critics point out that when stock
has already been sold, the owner may
receive the sale price, not what the
shares grew into. One legal journal
describes an owner who was offered
$8,000 for stock that had grown to
roughly $100,000.
For owners, the lesson is practical.
Searching costs nothing, and the money
can wait for you. For the state, the
lesson is stranger. Every dollar that a
rightful owner claims is a dollar
Delaware has to hand back. Step back and
the pattern is strange. The state is not
the owner of this money. It is a keeper
that is allowed to spend from the pot
while the owners are still missing. Most
of it is small and ordinary. A refund, a
deposit, an old check. Yet, add enough
of it together and a state of a million
people can lean on it for more than 6%
of its operating budget. The money is
not Delaware's, but Delaware's budget
has grown used to it. The rule that
decides where the money goes is not
about where it was earned or where the
owner lives. It comes down to one line
in a company's records. When that line
is empty, the money follows the
company's paperwork. Forgotten money has
to land somewhere and under American
law, it so often lands in Delaware.

When that line is empty, the money follows the company's paperwork. Forgotten money has to land somewhere and under American law, it so often lands in Delaware.

metadata.title: Delaware Makes More From Forgotten Money Than From Its Lottery
metadata.author: Lunch Cash
metadata.shortDescription:
Forgotten money doesn't disappear. A lot of it ends up in Delaware, and in 2025 it brought the state more than its lottery did.

When a company owes you money it can't deliver, a refund check you never cashed, a final paycheck, an old account, the law makes it hand the money to a state after a few years. Which state? The owner's last known address comes first. If the address line is blank, the money goes to the state where the company is incorporated, and more than two-thirds of the Fortune 500 are Delaware companies. We follow one forgotten $47 check (an example) to see where it lands, what Delaware does with it, and how you can get yours back for free.

Chapters
0:00 Forgotten Money
0:49 The Check
1:44 The Tag
3:02 Why Delaware
3:42 Delaware's Side
4:49 The Fights
6:04 The Vault
7:12 The Federal Drawer
7:53 Your Turn
9:20 Who Paid

The numbers (Delaware DEFAC General Fund revenue worksheet, May 2026, fiscal 2025 actual collections):
- Unclaimed property brought in $554.0 million. Refunds paid out of it came to $128.0 million. Net: $426.0 million.
- The lottery brought in $230.0 million.
- Our calculation: $128.0M of $554.0M is 23.1 percent, so for every four dollars that came in, less than one went back out as refunds. Same table, same year, same basis (General Fund).
- Delaware's own, different measure: the state says it returns on average between $150 million and $200 million a year to owners, counting cash and securities. That is not the same line as the budget's refunds, so we don't put the two into one ratio.
- Delaware's forecast for fiscal 2026 has refunds rising to $200.0 million (DEFAC, June 2026).
- Back in 2016, in one company's case about one audit, the federal court in Delaware wrote that "unclaimed property is Delaware's third largest revenue source" (Temple-Inland v. Cook). That describes 2016; Delaware has since rewritten its unclaimed property law (2017).
- Nationally, state unclaimed property programs returned more than $4.25 billion to owners in fiscal 2025 (NAUPA).
- About $35 billion in matured U.S. savings securities had not been cashed as of Sept 30, 2026 (Treasury). Treasury says savings bonds never expire.
- The $47 check is an example for illustration.

How to look for your own money:
1. Search missingmoney.com, an official site of the association of state unclaimed property offices (NAUPA), which searches participating states at once.
2. Also search your own state's official unclaimed property site, and Delaware's, if you've worked for or done business with big companies.
3. On official state sites, searching and claiming are free with the standard payment options. Some states, including Delaware, offer optional faster payouts for a fee.
4. Be careful with paid "finders". They usually take a percentage; some states limit their fees, and Delaware bans those deals in the first two years after the money reaches the state.
5. For old paper savings bonds, use the TreasuryDirect forms (for example FS Form 1048 for lost bonds). Treasury's old "Treasury Hunt" search tool is no longer available.
If anyone asks you to pay upfront to "release" unclaimed money, check with your state's official office first.

Delaware Code: 12 Del. C. ch. 11, subch. II; 29 Del. C. 6102
Delaware Division of Corporations, Annual Reports 2024 and 2025; Delaware news releases (Jan 30, 2025; Sept 9, 2025)
U.S. Supreme Court: Texas v. New Jersey (1965); Pennsylvania v. New York (1972); Delaware v. New York (1993); Delaware v. Pennsylvania (2023)
U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware: Temple-Inland Inc. v. Cook (2016)
NAUPA (National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators), FY2025 report and consumer guidance
U.S. Treasury: Monthly Statement of the Public Debt (Sept 30, 2026); 2024 SECURE 2.0 Act report to Congress (March 2025); TreasuryDirect
LaTurner v. United States, 933 F.3d 1354 (Fed. Cir. 2019)
Some scenes are dramatized and marked as such on screen.

Lunch Cash: complex stories, explained in bite-sized pieces. Subscribe, and find out who pays for lunch next.

Lunch Cash is not affiliated with or endorsed by the State of Delaware, NAUPA, MissingMoney.com or the U.S. Treasury. This video explains how unclaimed property works; it takes no position on any party or policy and is not legal or financial advice.

With states aggressively pursuing unclaimed property, our goal was to share practical guidance to help you to establish a sound reporting process and remain compliant.

Learn more about our State and Local Tax Practice, here: https://bit.ly/2W4swS7

metadata.title: Who Can Claim Unclaimed Property Of A Deceased Person?
metadata.author: Flying With Luxury
metadata.shortDescription:
Who Can Claim Unclaimed Property Of A Deceased Person?

1. Legal Authority First - Executor named in will gathers all assets legally, Administrator appointed by court manages estate without a will, Letters Testamentary or Administration prove claimant's legal authority.
2. Heirs-at-Law Claims - Heirs-at-law are closest relatives by state intestacy law, Surviving spouse, children, parents, then siblings typically claim, Provide death certificate, identity, relationship proof (affidavit).
3. The Claim Process - Search state treasury websites or NAUPA for property, Submit claim form with death certificate and authority proof, Strict verification prevents fraud, ensures rightful recovery of assets.
4. Important Considerations - Complex estates, multiple heirs, or missing heirs need guidance, Legal counsel helps navigate probate and heirship intricacies effectively, Without proper claims, property might escheat permanently to state.

Are you wondering how to file an unclaimed property claim as an heir? You're not alone! Many individuals find themselves in similar situations, seeking to claim assets left behind by loved ones or even distant relatives. This video is your complete guide to navigating the process with ease. From understanding the basics of unclaimed property to detailed steps on how to file your claim, we've got you covered. Discover crucial tips and secrets to ensure a smooth and successful journey as you lean into the opportunity to reclaim what's rightfully yours.

Being an heir can sometimes feel overwhelming, especially when dealing with the intricacies of unclaimed property. But fear not! This video walks you through each stage, providing clarity on legal documentation, probate processes, and how to deal with various state-specific regulations. We offer expert advice and practical insights so that by the end of this video, you'll have a comprehensive understanding of the entire claim process.

Disclaimer: This video is intended for informational purposes only and should not be construed as legal advice. The laws and regulations concerning unclaimed property claims can vary significantly by jurisdiction. It is advisable to consult with a qualified attorney or legal advisor for guidance tailored to your specific situation.

#OhioUnclaimedFunds #UnclaimedFunds #DivisionUnclaimedFunds
#DivisionUnclaimedFunds #OhioCommerce

What are unclaimed funds? Lost or forgotten money from inactive accounts that are reported by banks and businesses to the State of Ohio Division of Unclaimed Funds for safekeeping. Where does the money come from? inactive checking accounts, savings accounts, refund/credit balances, uncashed cashier’s checks, life insurance benefits, stocks & bonds, and safe deposit box contents. Business report unclaimed funds to us every year, per Ohio Revised Code 169. We have found that many of our claimants are over 50 years old and many more are already deceased. We need your help in getting your clients to claim their funds from an heir or trust as well as ensure Ohioans are regularly searching their names to make sure they don’t leave any behind. This webinar is meant to provide an overview on Unclaimed Funds in Ohio and how you can help your clients find and claim their money whether it’s for themselves or on behalf of a deceased loved one. After attending this webinar, you will learn: What are unclaimed funds, how to find out if you have any, and the steps to claiming funds, Claiming on behalf of a deceased family member and the required documentation, Claims timeline and delays, Claims status, and Claims resources. Visit unclaimedfunds.ohio.gov to search your name and claim your money today!
